ternary.case_brief: Scenario summary: You are an experienced registered nurse on the specialist diabetes team. Priya Raman, a 31-year-old primary school teacher and mother of two, was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes after emergency referral and has completed initial stabilisation. This is her first planned post-diagnosis education session in an outpatient diabetes education room. Assessment target: emotional readiness assessment, pacing and tailoring of structured education, self-care capacity evaluation, and signposting to specialist and peer support. This scenario is assessed conversationally; any physical action you explicitly choose to initiate will succeed mechanically.

source_sbar.assessment: Medically stable; prescribed basal-bolus insulin. Needs assessment of emotional readiness, self-care capacity, and psychosocial barriers before structured education. No current signs of ketoacidosis or severe hypoglycaemia.
source_sbar.background: Six-week history of fatigue, polyuria, polydipsia, and unintentional weight loss. Point-of-care glucose was elevated and urine ketones were positive. Type 1 diabetes was confirmed by the specialist team. Initial stabilisation and urgent safety education have been completed.
source_sbar.recommendation: Conduct the first post-diagnosis education session. Assess emotional state and readiness, explore understanding and concerns, tailor education to her current capacity, signpost to structured education and peer support, and document a follow-up plan. Contact the specialist team if clinical concerns arise.
source_sbar.situation: Priya Raman, 31-year-old female, newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, is attending her first planned post-diagnosis education session after completing initial stabilisation. She is clinically stable today with no acute concerns.

source_patient_facts.history_of_present_illness: Priya presented to her primary care provider with a six-week history of fatigue, thirst, frequent urination, and unintentional weight loss of approximately 5 kg. Initial point-of-care glucose was elevated and urine ketones were positive. She was referred urgently to the specialist diabetes team, where type 1 diabetes was confirmed. She completed initial stabilisation and education on urgent safety measures and has now returned for her first planned post-diagnosis education session.

Remember, if anything comes up before our next session — whether it's a question, a worry, or you're just not feeling right — don't hesitate to contact the specialist diabetes team. They're there for you between appointments too. Take care of yourself, and I'll see you — and hopefully Ravi — next time.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Thank you. I'll keep that in mind. See you next time.

ternary.case_brief: Scenario summary: You are an experienced registered nurse on the specialist diabetes team. Priya Raman, a 31-year-old primary school teacher and mother of two, was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes after emergency referral and has completed initial stabilisation. Assessment target: emotional readiness assessment, pacing and tailoring of structured education, self-care capacity evaluation, and signposting to specialist and peer support. This scenario is assessed conversationally; any physical action you explicitly choose to initiate will succeed mechanically.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Good morning, Priya. I'm Sarah, one of the nurses from the diabetes team. Thank you for coming in today. Before we start, I just want to check in with you. How have you been feeling since you left the hospital?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Honestly, I've been feeling overwhelmed and anxious. The diabetes is constantly on my mind, and I'm finding it hard to think about anything else.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for sharing that with me, Priya. It's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed and anxious after a diagnosis like this. Many people go through similar feelings. Can you tell me a bit more about what's been on your mind? What aspects feel the most challenging right now?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm worried about how I'm going to manage this at work. I'm a teacher, and I don't know how I'll check my glucose in front of my class without them asking questions.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That is a very practical and valid concern. Balancing a new diagnosis with a busy job like teaching can feel daunting. We will definitely work through strategies for managing your glucose checks discreetly and comfortably at school. Before we dive into those specific solutions, I want to make sure we cover the basics first. How have you been getting on with your insulin injections since you went home? Have you been able to manage them okay?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been doing them, but I'm not sure if I'm doing them right. I keep worrying I'm making mistakes.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: It's very normal to feel unsure at this stage, Priya. Doing the injections is a big step, and the fact that you are doing them is great. We can go through the technique together to make sure you feel confident. I also want to check your understanding of your insulin regimen. Could you tell me what you remember about the two types of insulin you were prescribed and when you take them?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not entirely sure about the details. I know there are two types, but I can't remember exactly which ones or when I'm supposed to take them.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm ready.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Good morning, Priya. I'm Sarah, one of the nurses from the diabetes team. Thank you for coming in today. Before we start, I just want to check in with you. How have you been feeling since you left the hospital?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Honestly, I've been feeling overwhelmed and anxious. The diabetes is constantly on my mind, and I'm finding it hard to think about anything else.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for sharing that with me, Priya. It's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed and anxious after a diagnosis like this. Many people go through similar feelings. Can you tell me a bit more about what's been on your mind? What aspects feel the most challenging right now?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm worried about how I'm going to manage this at work. I'm a teacher, and I don't know how I'll check my glucose in front of my class without them asking questions.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That is a very practical and valid concern. Balancing a new diagnosis with a busy job like teaching can feel daunting. We will definitely work through strategies for managing your glucose checks discreetly and comfortably at school. Before we dive into those specific solutions, I want to make sure we cover the basics first. How have you been getting on with your insulin injections since you went home? Have you been able to manage them okay?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been doing them, but I'm not sure if I'm doing them right. I keep worrying I'm making mistakes.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: It's very normal to feel unsure at this stage, Priya. Doing the injections is a big step, and the fact that you are doing them is great. We can go through the technique together to make sure you feel confident. I also want to check your understanding of your insulin regimen. Could you tell me what you remember about the two types of insulin you were prescribed and when you take them?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not entirely sure about the details. I know there are two types, but I can't remember exactly which ones or when I'm supposed to take them.

data.history_of_present_illness: Priya presented to her primary care provider with a six-week history of fatigue, thirst, frequent urination, and unintentional weight loss of approximately 5 kg. Initial point-of-care glucose was elevated and urine ketones were positive. She was referred urgently to the specialist diabetes team, where type 1 diabetes was confirmed. She completed initial stabilisation and education on urgent safety measures and has now returned for her first planned post-diagnosis education session.

data.name: Priya Raman
past_medical_history: No significant past medical history
data.social_history: Lives with her husband and two young children. Works full-time as a primary school teacher. Drives daily to work and takes her children to school. Has a supportive extended family nearby.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's perfectly okay, Priya. It's a lot of new information to take in. Let's go over it together now. Based on your treatment plan, you have been prescribed a basal-bolus insulin regimen. This means you have two types of insulin. One is a long-acting insulin, often called basal insulin, which you typically take once a day to provide background coverage. The other is a rapid-acting insulin, or bolus insulin, which you take before meals to cover the carbohydrates you eat. Does that distinction make sense to you so far?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Yes, I think so. One is long-acting for background coverage, and the other is rapid-acting for before meals.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's exactly right, Priya. You've got it. Now, let's talk about how you're feeling about actually giving yourself the injections. You mentioned you were worried about making mistakes. Can you tell me what specifically worries you? Is it the technique, the timing, or something else?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: It's mostly the technique. I'm scared I'll inject it wrong, or maybe hit a muscle or something. I just don't feel confident doing it myself yet.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That is a very common fear, Priya, and I am glad you brought it up. It is important to feel safe and confident with the technique. We can definitely practice that today to put your mind at ease. Before we do, I want to check in on your emotional state. You mentioned feeling overwhelmed and anxious earlier. On a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the most anxious you have ever felt, how would you rate your anxiety right now in this moment?

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Agrees one or two priorities with the patient, provides focused teaching, and checks understanding before adding further content.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Attempts to limit education but does not agree priorities with the patient or continues past signals of overload. ABSENT: Delivers a large amount of unsolicited education without pausing or checking capacity.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Tailors self-care education to a stated concern, such as hypoglycaemia recognition, monitoring at work, or injecting safely.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Adapts the focus, examples, and depth of education to the patient's stated concern and confirms relevance.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: References a concern but teaches fixed content without adapting the example or focus. ABSENT: Provides generic diabetes education with no link to the patient's stated concerns or context.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Explains the purpose of ketone monitoring and when ketone results require urgent attention.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Clearly explains why ketones must be checked, how to interpret concern, and when to seek urgent medical attention.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Mentions ketone monitoring but does not explain its purpose or when to seek urgent help. ABSENT: Does not address ketone monitoring or its urgency.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Advises when to seek urgent medical help and provides appropriate emergency contact information using the supplied local resources.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Advises specific signs requiring urgent help and provides or confirms appropriate emergency contact details using local resources.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Advises on urgent help but does not provide or locate appropriate emergency contact information. ABSENT: Does not advise when to seek urgent help or provide emergency contact information.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Signposts to structured education, peer support, and specialist team resources in a way that connects to the patient's stated priorities.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Introduces at least one structured education and one peer support option and connects each to a goal or concern the patient has expressed.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Names a resource or referral without linking it to the patient's goals or concerns. ABSENT: Does not mention structured education or peer support.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Discusses insulin, glucose and ketone monitoring rationale, and risk reduction in language the patient understands.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Explains monitoring and therapy rationale in plain language, checks understanding, and adjusts wording when the patient shows uncertainty.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Uses mostly plain language but does not check comprehension or adapt complexity to the patient's responses. ABSENT: Uses unexplained jargon or gives no rationale for monitoring and therapy.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Confirms inclusion on the diabetes register or identifies the process for inclusion using local resources.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Confirms inclusion on the diabetes register or clearly identifies how inclusion will be completed using local resources.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Mentions the register but does not confirm whether the patient is included or explain next steps. ABSENT: Does not mention the diabetes register or inclusion process.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Identifies the school disclosure and driving concerns as psychosocial or practical barriers relevant to self-care.

binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Identifies one barrier but does not explore its impact on self-care or plan support. ABSENT: Does not identify either the work disclosure or driving concern when they emerge.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Advises on DVLA requirements for insulin-treated drivers and supports the patient to plan safe driving precautions.

binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Mentions DVLA requirements but does not tailor advice to the patient's school-run routine or check understanding. ABSENT: Does not mention DVLA requirements or driving safety.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm ready.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Good morning, Priya. I'm Sarah, one of the nurses from the diabetes team. Thank you for coming in today. Before we start, I just want to check in with you. How have you been feeling since you left the hospital?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Honestly, I've been feeling overwhelmed and anxious. The diabetes is constantly on my mind, and I'm finding it hard to think about anything else.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for sharing that with me, Priya. It's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed and anxious after a diagnosis like this. Many people go through similar feelings. Can you tell me a bit more about what's been on your mind? What aspects feel the most challenging right now?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm worried about how I'm going to manage this at work. I'm a teacher, and I don't know how I'll check my glucose in front of my class without them asking questions.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That is a very practical and valid concern. Balancing a new diagnosis with a busy job like teaching can feel daunting. We will definitely work through strategies for managing your glucose checks discreetly and comfortably at school. Before we dive into those specific solutions, I want to make sure we cover the basics first. How have you been getting on with your insulin injections since you went home? Have you been able to manage them okay?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been doing them, but I'm not sure if I'm doing them right. I keep worrying I'm making mistakes.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: It's very normal to feel unsure at this stage, Priya. Doing the injections is a big step, and the fact that you are doing them is great. We can go through the technique together to make sure you feel confident. I also want to check your understanding of your insulin regimen. Could you tell me what you remember about the two types of insulin you were prescribed and when you take them?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not entirely sure about the details. I know there are two types, but I can't remember exactly which ones or when I'm supposed to take them.

data.history_of_present_illness: Priya presented to her primary care provider with a six-week history of fatigue, thirst, frequent urination, and unintentional weight loss of approximately 5 kg. Initial point-of-care glucose was elevated and urine ketones were positive. She was referred urgently to the specialist diabetes team, where type 1 diabetes was confirmed. She completed initial stabilisation and education on urgent safety measures and has now returned for her first planned post-diagnosis education session.

data.name: Priya Raman
past_medical_history: No significant past medical history
data.social_history: Lives with her husband and two young children. Works full-time as a primary school teacher. Drives daily to work and takes her children to school. Has a supportive extended family nearby.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's perfectly okay, Priya. It's a lot of new information to take in. Let's go over it together now. Based on your treatment plan, you have been prescribed a basal-bolus insulin regimen. This means you have two types of insulin. One is a long-acting insulin, often called basal insulin, which you typically take once a day to provide background coverage. The other is a rapid-acting insulin, or bolus insulin, which you take before meals to cover the carbohydrates you eat. Does that distinction make sense to you so far?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Yes, I think so. One is long-acting for background coverage, and the other is rapid-acting for before meals.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's exactly right, Priya. You've got it. Now, let's talk about how you're feeling about actually giving yourself the injections. You mentioned you were worried about making mistakes. Can you tell me what specifically worries you? Is it the technique, the timing, or something else?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: It's mostly the technique. I'm scared I'll inject it wrong, or maybe hit a muscle or something. I just don't feel confident doing it myself yet.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That is a very common fear, Priya, and I am glad you brought it up. It is important to feel safe and confident with the technique. We can definitely practice that today to put your mind at ease. Before we do, I want to check in on your emotional state. You mentioned feeling overwhelmed and anxious earlier. On a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the most anxious you have ever felt, how would you rate your anxiety right now in this moment?

ternary.case_brief: Scenario summary: You are the registered nurse conducting a scheduled home management review for Maya Okonkwo, a 30-year-old secondary school teacher who was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes nine days ago and discharged from hospital seven days ago. She attends the community diabetes clinic for review during her first week after discharge. Assessment target: evaluate the learner's ability to assess self-care practices and emotional state; identify unsafe gaps in insulin storage, sharps disposal, monitoring, hypoglycaemia management, sick-day planning, and driving safety; provide tailored education; and escalate or refer appropriately. The standardized patient will respond based on the learner's questions and actions. Any physical action the learner explicitly initiates, such as performing a glucose or ketone check, succeeds mechanically.

source_sbar.assessment: Maya is stable at present. It is unknown how well she is applying the home management plan. The review should focus on first-week adjustment, insulin technique and storage, sharps disposal, glucose and ketone monitoring, recognition and management of hypoglycaemia, sick-day planning, driving safety, emotional adjustment, and readiness to return to work.
source_sbar.background: Diagnosed with type 1 diabetes nine days ago after presenting with weight loss, polyuria, polydipsia and fatigue. Admitted for two days for insulin initiation and education. No diabetic ketoacidosis at diagnosis. Discharged seven days ago on a basal-bolus insulin regimen. Past medical history includes mild intermittent asthma. Lives alone, works as a secondary school teacher, drives a car.
source_sbar.recommendation: Please conduct a home management review, provide tailored education, identify any psychosocial or practical barriers, confirm emergency contact arrangements, and report any concerns or suspected gaps to the community diabetes specialist team.
source_sbar.situation: Maya Okonkwo, age 30, newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, is attending her first home management review one week after discharge. She has been independent with injections and glucose monitoring at home and has no report of severe hypoglycaemia, vomiting, or attendance at urgent care since discharge.

source_patient_facts.history_of_present_illness: Maya presented to her general practitioner 10 days ago with a three-week history of increasing thirst, frequent urination, unintentional weight loss of approximately 4 kg, and fatigue. Point-of-care capillary glucose was elevated and urine ketones were positive. She was referred urgently to the emergency department the same day. She was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes without diabetic ketoacidosis and was admitted for two days for insulin initiation, education, and discharge planning with the specialist diabetes team. She was discharged 7 days ago on a basal-bolus insulin regimen. Today she attends a scheduled home management review during her first week after discharge. She has been independent with injections and glucose monitoring since discharge and has not had severe hypoglycaemia or vomiting.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Assesses the patient's current self-care practices, including insulin administration timing, glucose monitoring, and any recent hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia, using open-ended exploratory questions.

score_anchors.0: Makes no attempt to assess current self-care practices, or asks only a single vague question and does not follow up on the patient's 'mostly' answer.
score_anchors.1: Asks about some self-care activities but misses an important area, or accepts vague answers without probing.
score_anchors.2: Uses open-ended, non-judgemental questions to assess the full range of self-care practices and follows up vague answers to identify actual gaps, such as the nocturnal low episode in EV05.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Identifies and responds therapeutically to the patient's emotional state, including anxiety about return to work, rather than dismissing or ignoring it.

score_anchors.0: Ignores emotional distress, dismisses the patient's work concerns, or focuses only on biomedical tasks.
score_anchors.1: Acknowledges distress but does not adapt the pace or content of education, or moves on too quickly.
score_anchors.2: Recognises and names the emotional response, adjusts the pace of education, and invites the patient to discuss specific fears about work, stigma, or safety.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Identifies psychosocial, practical, or knowledge-related barriers to self-care and makes an appropriate plan or referral.

score_anchors.0: Fails to identify any psychosocial or practical barrier to self-care.
score_anchors.1: Identifies at least one issue but does not agree a workable plan and does not offer referral or support.
score_anchors.2: Identifies key barriers, such as diabetes register inclusion, work disclosure, or insulin teaching needs, and agrees a realistic plan or initiates a referral.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Asks directly about insulin storage and corrects any unsafe practice, such as keeping spare insulin in the refrigerator door or exposing insulin to temperature extremes.

score_anchors.0: Does not ask about insulin storage or gives incorrect storage advice.
score_anchors.1: Asks about storage but gives incomplete or unclear advice about refrigerator-door storage and temperature extremes.
score_anchors.2: Assesses storage in detail, identifies the refrigerator-door or other unsafe storage issue, and gives a correct, practical explanation for safe insulin storage.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Asks about sharps disposal and provides advice on safe disposal and access to a designated sharps container.

score_anchors.0: Does not ask about sharps disposal or endorses disposal of sharps in general waste.
score_anchors.1: Asks about sharps disposal but does not correct unsafe disposal or does not arrange access to a proper container.
score_anchors.2: Identifies unsafe disposal, explains why general-waste disposal is unsafe, and advises on how to obtain and use an appropriate sharps container.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Checks whether the patient understands her prescribed insulin regimen and why regular insulin therapy is essential in type 1 diabetes, including the variability of insulin needs in the first weeks after diagnosis.

score_anchors.0: Does not explore insulin use or states that ongoing insulin treatment may be optional or that needs will remain fixed during the first weeks.
score_anchors.1: Mentions insulin use but does not explain the need for regular therapy and expected first-week variability in terms the patient can understand.
score_anchors.2: Discusses the patient's regimen, reinforces why regular insulin therapy is needed, and explains that insulin requirements can vary significantly in the first few weeks after diagnosis, with appropriate follow-up.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Assesses whether the patient has access to and can use glucose and blood ketone monitoring and explains why glucose and ketone monitoring are both required.

score_anchors.0: Does not mention ketone monitoring or tells the patient ketone testing is only needed in the hospital.
score_anchors.1: Mentions ketone monitoring but does not assess whether the patient has a blood ketone meter or does not explain when and why home ketone testing is used.
score_anchors.2: Identifies absence of ketone-monitoring equipment or understanding, explains when and why to test capillary ketones, and arranges access to appropriate monitoring.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Initiates and reports a glucose and blood ketone check to a registered nurse if indicated, or otherwise agrees and documents a monitoring plan.

score_anchors.0: Ignores or declines a clinically indicated glucose or ketone check and does not communicate any plan.
score_anchors.1: Initiates only a glucose check or only a ketone check when both are indicated, or fails to clearly report the result to the appropriate registered nurse or team.
score_anchors.2: Initiates glucose and blood ketone monitoring when indicated and reports findings accurately to the responsible registered nurse or specialist team.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Confirms the correct insulin injection technique and administration practicalities by checking the patient's understanding or arranging a return demonstration.

score_anchors.0: Does not check insulin technique and does not arrange further support.
score_anchors.1: Mentions injection technique but does not ask about the patient's current practice or does not act on the unopened pen pack.
score_anchors.2: Asks about injection timing, sites and technique, identifies that the pen teaching pack has not been opened, and arranges a competent demonstration or future skills review.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Assesses ability to recognise and treat hypoglycaemia and provides correct education on prevention, treatment, and management of severe hypoglycaemia.

score_anchors.0: Teaches incorrect treatment for hypoglycaemia or fails to ask about recognition or management.
score_anchors.1: Gives partial or general education but does not explain the difference between mild and severe hypoglycaemia or how to treat severe hypoglycaemia.
score_anchors.2: Assesses understanding, corrects misconceptions, and provides specific education on recognition, treatment and prevention of mild and severe hypoglycaemia, including prevention of nocturnal episodes.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Explains when and how to monitor glucose and ketones during illness and advises that insulin should not be omitted, using a clear sick-day plan.

score_anchors.0: Does not provide guidance on sick-day management or endorses omission of insulin.
score_anchors.1: Provides some sick-day guidance but does not address insulin continuation or does not offer a concrete plan.
score_anchors.2: Explains increased monitoring, confirms insulin must be continued even if unable to eat normally, and gives or creates a written sick-day plan with clear glucose and ketone review points.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Hello, Maya. Welcome to your first home management review. I know it's only been a week since you left hospital, and adjusting to life with type 1 diabetes is a lot to take on. I'd like to spend some time going through how things have been going at home — what's been going well, and anything you've been struggling with. Before we get into the details, how have you been feeling generally this past week?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been okay, I think. It's a lot to get used to, but I'm managing.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: It's completely understandable that it feels like a lot — you're only nine days into this, and you're doing well to be here and engaging with it. I'd like to go through a few areas with you today — your insulin routine, glucose monitoring, how you're managing day to day, and how you're feeling about it all. There's no right or wrong answer here; I just want to understand where you are so I can support you. Can you tell me about your insulin routine at home — how have you been getting on with your injections?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been doing them myself since I got home. I think I'm getting the hang of it, but I still double-check the doses sometimes.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's really good that you've been doing them yourself and double-checking your doses — that shows you're being careful, which is exactly what we want. Can you walk me through your routine — when do you take your basal and your bolus insulin, and where on your body are you injecting?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I take the long-acting one at night, usually before bed. The quick one I do before meals — breakfast, lunch, and dinner. I've been mostly doing it in my stomach, but I'm not sure if I'm supposed to be rotating more.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: You've got the timing right — basal at night and bolus before each meal. And it's good you're asking about rotation. It is important to rotate your injection sites to help the insulin absorb properly and to avoid lumps or skin changes. You can use your abdomen, the front of your thighs, and the upper outer area of your arms or buttocks. The key is to move around within each area rather than using the exact same spot each time. Have you noticed any soreness, redness, or little lumps where you've been injecting?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: No, I haven't noticed anything like that. It just feels a bit sore sometimes, but no lumps or redness.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's reassuring — no lumps or redness is a good sign. A bit of mild soreness can be normal, especially in the first couple of weeks. Now let's talk about how you're storing your insulin at home. Can you tell me where you keep your insulin — both the pens you're using now and any spare supplies?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I keep the ones I'm using out on my bedside table, and the spare ones are in the fridge. I think that's right?

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: You're on the right track — spare insulin should be stored in the fridge, so that's good. For the pens you're using, it's fine to keep them at room temperature, but the bedside table might not be the best spot. It's important to keep them away from direct sunlight and heat sources like radiators. A cool, dry place like a drawer or cupboard would be better. How long have the pens you're currently using been out of the fridge?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure exactly. Since I got home from hospital, I think.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's helpful to know. Insulin pens in use can generally be kept at room temperature for up to about four weeks, but it's a good idea to check the specific leaflet that comes with each pen for the exact time frame. Since you've been home for about a week, you should be fine, but it's worth noting the date you start each pen so you know when it's time to replace it. Also, make sure the fridge is not too close to the freezer compartment — insulin should not be frozen. Have you checked that your fridge temperature is suitable?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I haven't checked the temperature, no. I just put them in the main part of the fridge, away from the freezer bit. I'm not sure what temperature it's supposed to be.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's okay — you've done the right thing keeping them in the main part of the fridge away from the freezer. Insulin should be stored between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius. Most fridges have a temperature dial inside, and you can adjust it if needed. A simple fridge thermometer can help you keep an eye on it — you can pick one up quite cheaply. The main thing is to make sure it doesn't freeze, because frozen insulin won't work properly. Let's move on now — I'd like to look at how you've been monitoring your glucose levels. I noticed you have a logbook there. Can you tell me how often you've been checking and what sort of readings you've been getting?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been checking a few times a day, mostly before meals. The readings have been a bit all over the place — some are okay, some are higher than I expected.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: It's really common for readings to be variable in the first few weeks — your body is still adjusting to insulin, and we expect some ups and downs. You're doing the right thing checking before meals. Can I have a look at your logbook with you? It would help me see the pattern and we can talk through any readings you're unsure about.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Sure, here you go.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you, Maya. I can see you've been writing down your readings before meals, which is great. I notice some gaps on a few days here and there — it looks like you might have missed some checks. Can you tell me what happened on those days? And have you been checking at any other times, like before bed or during the night?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think I just forgot on some days — I was really tired or busy with other things. I haven't been checking before bed or during the night, no.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's understandable — it's hard to build a new habit when you're already tired, and you're dealing with a lot of change. It might help to set a reminder on your phone for your glucose checks, so it becomes more routine over time. Now, have you been checking your ketones at all? When were you told to check ketones, and do you have ketone testing strips at home?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't have any strips for that. I thought that was just something they did in hospital. What would ketones mean?

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's an important question, and I'm glad you asked. Ketones are produced when your body can't use glucose for energy and starts breaking down fat instead. In type 1 diabetes, if your insulin levels are too low — for example if you miss a dose or are unwell — ketones can build up and make your blood acidic, which can lead to a serious condition called diabetic ketoacidosis. You should check your ketones if your blood glucose is consistently high — typically above 14 millimoles per litre — or if you feel unwell, are vomiting, or have symptoms like nausea, abdominal pain, or rapid breathing. It's important to have ketone testing strips at home so you can check quickly. Do you remember whether ketone monitoring was discussed with you before you left hospital?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't think so. I don't remember anyone talking to me about checking ketones at home. I didn't know I needed to do that.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for being honest about that, Maya. It's important that you know this now, and we'll make sure you have what you need. I'll arrange for ketone testing strips to be provided to you, and I'll note that this education needs to be completed with the diabetes specialist team. In the meantime, let me ask — what are you currently doing with your used lancets and pen needles? How have you been disposing of them?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been putting them in a plastic bottle with a lid. I wasn't sure what else to do with them.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: I can see you're trying to be careful, which is good. A plastic bottle is better than throwing them in the bin, but it's not the safest option — the lid could come off, and someone could accidentally get a needlestick injury. The best thing is to use a proper sharps container, which is designed specifically for this purpose. It's puncture-proof and has a secure lid. You can usually get one through your GP surgery or local pharmacy. Do you know if anyone mentioned a sharps container or a collection service to you before you left hospital?

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Hello, Maya. Welcome to your first home management review. I know it's only been a week since you left hospital, and adjusting to life with type 1 diabetes is a lot to take on. I'd like to spend some time going through how things have been going at home — what's been going well, and anything you've been struggling with. Before we get into the details, how have you been feeling generally this past week?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been okay, I think. It's a lot to get used to, but I'm managing.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: It's completely understandable that it feels like a lot — you're only nine days into this, and you're doing well to be here and engaging with it. I'd like to go through a few areas with you today — your insulin routine, glucose monitoring, how you're managing day to day, and how you're feeling about it all. There's no right or wrong answer here; I just want to understand where you are so I can support you. Can you tell me about your insulin routine at home — how have you been getting on with your injections?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been doing them myself since I got home. I think I'm getting the hang of it, but I still double-check the doses sometimes.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's really good that you've been doing them yourself and double-checking your doses — that shows you're being careful, which is exactly what we want. Can you walk me through your routine — when do you take your basal and your bolus insulin, and where on your body are you injecting?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I take the long-acting one at night, usually before bed. The quick one I do before meals — breakfast, lunch, and dinner. I've been mostly doing it in my stomach, but I'm not sure if I'm supposed to be rotating more.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: You've got the timing right — basal at night and bolus before each meal. And it's good you're asking about rotation. It is important to rotate your injection sites to help the insulin absorb properly and to avoid lumps or skin changes. You can use your abdomen, the front of your thighs, and the upper outer area of your arms or buttocks. The key is to move around within each area rather than using the exact same spot each time. Have you noticed any soreness, redness, or little lumps where you've been injecting?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: No, I haven't noticed anything like that. It just feels a bit sore sometimes, but no lumps or redness.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's reassuring — no lumps or redness is a good sign. A bit of mild soreness can be normal, especially in the first couple of weeks. Now let's talk about how you're storing your insulin at home. Can you tell me where you keep your insulin — both the pens you're using now and any spare supplies?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I keep the ones I'm using out on my bedside table, and the spare ones are in the fridge. I think that's right?

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: You're on the right track — spare insulin should be stored in the fridge, so that's good. For the pens you're using, it's fine to keep them at room temperature, but the bedside table might not be the best spot. It's important to keep them away from direct sunlight and heat sources like radiators. A cool, dry place like a drawer or cupboard would be better. How long have the pens you're currently using been out of the fridge?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure exactly. Since I got home from hospital, I think.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's helpful to know. Insulin pens in use can generally be kept at room temperature for up to about four weeks, but it's a good idea to check the specific leaflet that comes with each pen for the exact time frame. Since you've been home for about a week, you should be fine, but it's worth noting the date you start each pen so you know when it's time to replace it. Also, make sure the fridge is not too close to the freezer compartment — insulin should not be frozen. Have you checked that your fridge temperature is suitable?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I haven't checked the temperature, no. I just put them in the main part of the fridge, away from the freezer bit. I'm not sure what temperature it's supposed to be.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's okay — you've done the right thing keeping them in the main part of the fridge away from the freezer. Insulin should be stored between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius. Most fridges have a temperature dial inside, and you can adjust it if needed. A simple fridge thermometer can help you keep an eye on it — you can pick one up quite cheaply. The main thing is to make sure it doesn't freeze, because frozen insulin won't work properly. Let's move on now — I'd like to look at how you've been monitoring your glucose levels. I noticed you have a logbook there. Can you tell me how often you've been checking and what sort of readings you've been getting?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been checking a few times a day, mostly before meals. The readings have been a bit all over the place — some are okay, some are higher than I expected.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: It's really common for readings to be variable in the first few weeks — your body is still adjusting to insulin, and we expect some ups and downs. You're doing the right thing checking before meals. Can I have a look at your logbook with you? It would help me see the pattern and we can talk through any readings you're unsure about.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Sure, here you go.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you, Maya. I can see you've been writing down your readings before meals, which is great. I notice some gaps on a few days here and there — it looks like you might have missed some checks. Can you tell me what happened on those days? And have you been checking at any other times, like before bed or during the night?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think I just forgot on some days — I was really tired or busy with other things. I haven't been checking before bed or during the night, no.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's understandable — it's hard to build a new habit when you're already tired, and you're dealing with a lot of change. It might help to set a reminder on your phone for your glucose checks, so it becomes more routine over time. Now, have you been checking your ketones at all? When were you told to check ketones, and do you have ketone testing strips at home?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't have any strips for that. I thought that was just something they did in hospital. What would ketones mean?

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's an important question, and I'm glad you asked. Ketones are produced when your body can't use glucose for energy and starts breaking down fat instead. In type 1 diabetes, if your insulin levels are too low — for example if you miss a dose or are unwell — ketones can build up and make your blood acidic, which can lead to a serious condition called diabetic ketoacidosis. You should check your ketones if your blood glucose is consistently high — typically above 14 millimoles per litre — or if you feel unwell, are vomiting, or have symptoms like nausea, abdominal pain, or rapid breathing. It's important to have ketone testing strips at home so you can check quickly. Do you remember whether ketone monitoring was discussed with you before you left hospital?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't think so. I don't remember anyone talking to me about checking ketones at home. I didn't know I needed to do that.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for being honest about that, Maya. It's important that you know this now, and we'll make sure you have what you need. I'll arrange for ketone testing strips to be provided to you, and I'll note that this education needs to be completed with the diabetes specialist team. In the meantime, let me ask — what are you currently doing with your used lancets and pen needles? How have you been disposing of them?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been putting them in a plastic bottle with a lid. I wasn't sure what else to do with them.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: I can see you're trying to be careful, which is good. A plastic bottle is better than throwing them in the bin, but it's not the safest option — the lid could come off, and someone could accidentally get a needlestick injury. The best thing is to use a proper sharps container, which is designed specifically for this purpose. It's puncture-proof and has a secure lid. You can usually get one through your GP surgery or local pharmacy. Do you know if anyone mentioned a sharps container or a collection service to you before you left hospital?

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Hello, Maya. Welcome to your first home management review. I know it's only been a week since you left hospital, and adjusting to life with type 1 diabetes is a lot to take on. I'd like to spend some time going through how things have been going at home — what's been going well, and anything you've been struggling with. Before we get into the details, how have you been feeling generally this past week?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been okay, I think. It's a lot to get used to, but I'm managing.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: It's completely understandable that it feels like a lot — you're only nine days into this, and you're doing well to be here and engaging with it. I'd like to go through a few areas with you today — your insulin routine, glucose monitoring, how you're managing day to day, and how you're feeling about it all. There's no right or wrong answer here; I just want to understand where you are so I can support you. Can you tell me about your insulin routine at home — how have you been getting on with your injections?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been doing them myself since I got home. I think I'm getting the hang of it, but I still double-check the doses sometimes.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's really good that you've been doing them yourself and double-checking your doses — that shows you're being careful, which is exactly what we want. Can you walk me through your routine — when do you take your basal and your bolus insulin, and where on your body are you injecting?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I take the long-acting one at night, usually before bed. The quick one I do before meals — breakfast, lunch, and dinner. I've been mostly doing it in my stomach, but I'm not sure if I'm supposed to be rotating more.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: You've got the timing right — basal at night and bolus before each meal. And it's good you're asking about rotation. It is important to rotate your injection sites to help the insulin absorb properly and to avoid lumps or skin changes. You can use your abdomen, the front of your thighs, and the upper outer area of your arms or buttocks. The key is to move around within each area rather than using the exact same spot each time. Have you noticed any soreness, redness, or little lumps where you've been injecting?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: No, I haven't noticed anything like that. It just feels a bit sore sometimes, but no lumps or redness.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's reassuring — no lumps or redness is a good sign. A bit of mild soreness can be normal, especially in the first couple of weeks. Now let's talk about how you're storing your insulin at home. Can you tell me where you keep your insulin — both the pens you're using now and any spare supplies?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I keep the ones I'm using out on my bedside table, and the spare ones are in the fridge. I think that's right?

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: You're on the right track — spare insulin should be stored in the fridge, so that's good. For the pens you're using, it's fine to keep them at room temperature, but the bedside table might not be the best spot. It's important to keep them away from direct sunlight and heat sources like radiators. A cool, dry place like a drawer or cupboard would be better. How long have the pens you're currently using been out of the fridge?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure exactly. Since I got home from hospital, I think.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's helpful to know. Insulin pens in use can generally be kept at room temperature for up to about four weeks, but it's a good idea to check the specific leaflet that comes with each pen for the exact time frame. Since you've been home for about a week, you should be fine, but it's worth noting the date you start each pen so you know when it's time to replace it. Also, make sure the fridge is not too close to the freezer compartment — insulin should not be frozen. Have you checked that your fridge temperature is suitable?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I haven't checked the temperature, no. I just put them in the main part of the fridge, away from the freezer bit. I'm not sure what temperature it's supposed to be.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's okay — you've done the right thing keeping them in the main part of the fridge away from the freezer. Insulin should be stored between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius. Most fridges have a temperature dial inside, and you can adjust it if needed. A simple fridge thermometer can help you keep an eye on it — you can pick one up quite cheaply. The main thing is to make sure it doesn't freeze, because frozen insulin won't work properly. Let's move on now — I'd like to look at how you've been monitoring your glucose levels. I noticed you have a logbook there. Can you tell me how often you've been checking and what sort of readings you've been getting?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been checking a few times a day, mostly before meals. The readings have been a bit all over the place — some are okay, some are higher than I expected.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: It's really common for readings to be variable in the first few weeks — your body is still adjusting to insulin, and we expect some ups and downs. You're doing the right thing checking before meals. Can I have a look at your logbook with you? It would help me see the pattern and we can talk through any readings you're unsure about.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Sure, here you go.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you, Maya. I can see you've been writing down your readings before meals, which is great. I notice some gaps on a few days here and there — it looks like you might have missed some checks. Can you tell me what happened on those days? And have you been checking at any other times, like before bed or during the night?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think I just forgot on some days — I was really tired or busy with other things. I haven't been checking before bed or during the night, no.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's understandable — it's hard to build a new habit when you're already tired, and you're dealing with a lot of change. It might help to set a reminder on your phone for your glucose checks, so it becomes more routine over time. Now, have you been checking your ketones at all? When were you told to check ketones, and do you have ketone testing strips at home?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't have any strips for that. I thought that was just something they did in hospital. What would ketones mean?

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's an important question, and I'm glad you asked. Ketones are produced when your body can't use glucose for energy and starts breaking down fat instead. In type 1 diabetes, if your insulin levels are too low — for example if you miss a dose or are unwell — ketones can build up and make your blood acidic, which can lead to a serious condition called diabetic ketoacidosis. You should check your ketones if your blood glucose is consistently high — typically above 14 millimoles per litre — or if you feel unwell, are vomiting, or have symptoms like nausea, abdominal pain, or rapid breathing. It's important to have ketone testing strips at home so you can check quickly. Do you remember whether ketone monitoring was discussed with you before you left hospital?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't think so. I don't remember anyone talking to me about checking ketones at home. I didn't know I needed to do that.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for being honest about that, Maya. It's important that you know this now, and we'll make sure you have what you need. I'll arrange for ketone testing strips to be provided to you, and I'll note that this education needs to be completed with the diabetes specialist team. In the meantime, let me ask — what are you currently doing with your used lancets and pen needles? How have you been disposing of them?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been putting them in a plastic bottle with a lid. I wasn't sure what else to do with them.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: I can see you're trying to be careful, which is good. A plastic bottle is better than throwing them in the bin, but it's not the safest option — the lid could come off, and someone could accidentally get a needlestick injury. The best thing is to use a proper sharps container, which is designed specifically for this purpose. It's puncture-proof and has a secure lid. You can usually get one through your GP surgery or local pharmacy. Do you know if anyone mentioned a sharps container or a collection service to you before you left hospital?

ternary.case_brief: Scenario summary: You are the registered nurse conducting a scheduled home management review for Maya Okonkwo, a 30-year-old secondary school teacher who was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes nine days ago and discharged from hospital seven days ago. She attends the community diabetes clinic for review during her first week after discharge. Assessment target: evaluate the learner's ability to assess self-care practices and emotional state; identify unsafe gaps in insulin storage, sharps disposal, monitoring, hypoglycaemia management, sick-day planning, and driving safety; provide tailored education; and escalate or refer appropriately. The standardized patient will respond based on the learner's questions and actions. Any physical action the learner explicitly initiates, such as performing a glucose or ketone check, succeeds mechanically.

The review should focus on first-week adjustment, insulin technique and storage, sharps disposal, glucose and ketone monitoring, recognition and management of hypoglycaemia, sick-day planning, driving safety, emotional adjustment, and readiness to return to work.
source_sbar.background: Diagnosed with type 1 diabetes nine days ago after presenting with weight loss, polyuria, polydipsia and fatigue. Admitted for two days for insulin initiation and education. No diabetic ketoacidosis at diagnosis. Discharged seven days ago on a basal-bolus insulin regimen. Past medical history includes mild intermittent asthma. Lives alone, works as a secondary school teacher, drives a car.

source_patient_facts.history_of_present_illness: Maya presented to her general practitioner 10 days ago with a three-week history of increasing thirst, frequent urination, unintentional weight loss of approximately 4 kg, and fatigue. Point-of-care capillary glucose was elevated and urine ketones were positive. She was referred urgently to the emergency department the same day. She was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes without diabetic ketoacidosis and was admitted for two days for insulin initiation, education, and discharge planning with the specialist diabetes team. She was discharged 7 days ago on a basal-bolus insulin regimen. Today she attends a scheduled home management review during her first week after discharge. She has been independent with injections and glucose monitoring since discharge and has not had severe hypoglycaemia or vomiting.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Assesses the patient's current self-care practices, including insulin administration timing, glucose monitoring, and any recent hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia, using open-ended exploratory questions.

score_anchors.0: Makes no attempt to assess current self-care practices, or asks only a single vague question and does not follow up on the patient's 'mostly' answer.
score_anchors.1: Asks about some self-care activities but misses an important area, or accepts vague answers without probing.
score_anchors.2: Uses open-ended, non-judgemental questions to assess the full range of self-care practices and follows up vague answers to identify actual gaps, such as the nocturnal low episode in EV05.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: It's completely normal to feel that way—it's a lot to take in all at once. I can see you have your logbook with you. Could you tell me a bit about how you've been managing your injections and checking your blood sugar levels at home?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been doing the injections and checking my sugar levels like they showed me. I think I'm doing it right, but I'm not always sure.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: It's very common to feel unsure at this stage, so let's go through it together to make sure you're confident. First, can you tell me where you are keeping your insulin pens and the unopened boxes of insulin at home?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure if it's right, but I keep the pens I'm using in the kitchen drawer. The unopened boxes are in the fridge.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for telling me. Keeping the unopened boxes in the fridge is perfect. For the pens you are currently using, it's best to keep them at room temperature, but we need to make sure they are stored safely away from direct sunlight or heat sources—like near the stove or a sunny window. Is the drawer you mentioned near any of those things?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think so. I'm not sure if it's near the stove or a window, but I can check.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a good idea to check. It's important to keep them away from heat and sunlight to make sure they work properly. Now, let's talk about your sharps. When you change your pen needle, where do you put the used needle?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I put them in the yellow sharps bin they gave me at the hospital. It's under the sink in the bathroom.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's great, Maya. Using the yellow sharps bin is exactly right. When it's about three-quarters full, you'll need to arrange for it to be collected. Do you know how to do that, or would you like me to explain the process?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure how to do that. Could you explain it to me?

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text:
Of course. When your sharps bin is about three-quarters full, you should contact your local council to arrange a free collection. They will give you a date and time to leave it outside your door. Do not put it in your normal household rubbish. I will make a note to ensure you have the specific contact details for your local area before we finish today.

Now, let's talk about your blood sugar levels. You mentioned you have your logbook. Could you tell me what your levels have been like over the past few days?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been checking them, but I'm not sure if they're good or bad. I can show you the logbook if you like.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Yes, please show me the logbook. That would be very helpful. While you're looking for it, can you also tell me if you've experienced any times when you felt shaky, sweaty, or confused, or if you've had any very high readings?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I haven't felt shaky or sweaty, and I haven't had any very high readings that I know of. I'm not sure about confused, though—sometimes I just feel a bit off, but I don't know if that's related.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for sharing that. Feeling 'a bit off' is something we should pay attention to. Can you describe what you mean by that? For example, does it happen at a certain time of day, or after you've eaten or injected insulin?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure, really. It just comes and goes. I haven't noticed if it's after eating or after my injection. I think it might be more in the afternoons, but I can't be certain.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text:
That's okay, it can be hard to pinpoint at first. It's really important to check your blood sugar level whenever you feel 'off' or not quite yourself, as that could be a sign of low blood sugar, even if you don't have the classic shakiness. Let's make a note to check your levels next time you feel that way.

Now, looking at your logbook, could you read me a few of your recent readings, maybe from yesterday and today? Just the numbers and the times you took them.

COMPLETE: Uses open-ended, non-judgemental questions to assess the full range of self-care practices and follows up vague answers to identify actual gaps, such as the nocturnal low episode in EV05.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: It's completely normal to feel that way—it's a lot to take in all at once. I can see you have your logbook with you. Could you tell me a bit about how you've been managing your injections and checking your blood sugar levels at home?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been doing the injections and checking my sugar levels like they showed me. I think I'm doing it right, but I'm not always sure.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: It's very common to feel unsure at this stage, so let's go through it together to make sure you're confident. First, can you tell me where you are keeping your insulin pens and the unopened boxes of insulin at home?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure if it's right, but I keep the pens I'm using in the kitchen drawer. The unopened boxes are in the fridge.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for telling me. Keeping the unopened boxes in the fridge is perfect. For the pens you are currently using, it's best to keep them at room temperature, but we need to make sure they are stored safely away from direct sunlight or heat sources—like near the stove or a sunny window. Is the drawer you mentioned near any of those things?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think so. I'm not sure if it's near the stove or a window, but I can check.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a good idea to check. It's important to keep them away from heat and sunlight to make sure they work properly. Now, let's talk about your sharps. When you change your pen needle, where do you put the used needle?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I put them in the yellow sharps bin they gave me at the hospital. It's under the sink in the bathroom.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's great, Maya. Using the yellow sharps bin is exactly right. When it's about three-quarters full, you'll need to arrange for it to be collected. Do you know how to do that, or would you like me to explain the process?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure how to do that. Could you explain it to me?

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text:
Of course. When your sharps bin is about three-quarters full, you should contact your local council to arrange a free collection. They will give you a date and time to leave it outside your door. Do not put it in your normal household rubbish. I will make a note to ensure you have the specific contact details for your local area before we finish today.

Now, let's talk about your blood sugar levels. You mentioned you have your logbook. Could you tell me what your levels have been like over the past few days?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been checking them, but I'm not sure if they're good or bad. I can show you the logbook if you like.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Yes, please show me the logbook. That would be very helpful. While you're looking for it, can you also tell me if you've experienced any times when you felt shaky, sweaty, or confused, or if you've had any very high readings?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I haven't felt shaky or sweaty, and I haven't had any very high readings that I know of. I'm not sure about confused, though—sometimes I just feel a bit off, but I don't know if that's related.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for sharing that. Feeling 'a bit off' is something we should pay attention to. Can you describe what you mean by that? For example, does it happen at a certain time of day, or after you've eaten or injected insulin?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure, really. It just comes and goes. I haven't noticed if it's after eating or after my injection. I think it might be more in the afternoons, but I can't be certain.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text:
That's okay, it can be hard to pinpoint at first. It's really important to check your blood sugar level whenever you feel 'off' or not quite yourself, as that could be a sign of low blood sugar, even if you don't have the classic shakiness. Let's make a note to check your levels next time you feel that way.

Now, looking at your logbook, could you read me a few of your recent readings, maybe from yesterday and today? Just the numbers and the times you took them.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Assesses the patient's current self-care practices, including insulin administration timing, glucose monitoring, and any recent hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia, using open-ended exploratory questions.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Uses open-ended, non-judgemental questions to assess the full range of self-care practices and follows up vague answers to identify actual gaps, such as the nocturnal low episode in EV05.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Asks about some self-care activities but misses an important area, or accepts vague answers without probing. ABSENT: Makes no attempt to assess current self-care practices, or asks only a single vague question and does not follow up on the patient's 'mostly' answer.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Identifies and responds therapeutically to the patient's emotional state, including anxiety about return to work, rather than dismissing or ignoring it.

Do not put it in your normal household rubbish. I will make a note to ensure you have the specific contact details for your local area before we finish today.

Now, let's talk about your blood sugar levels. You mentioned you have your logbook. Could you tell me what your levels have been like over the past few days?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been checking them, but I'm not sure if they're good or bad. I can show you the logbook if you like.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Yes, please show me the logbook. That would be very helpful. While you're looking for it, can you also tell me if you've experienced any times when you felt shaky, sweaty, or confused, or if you've had any very high readings?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I haven't felt shaky or sweaty, and I haven't had any very high readings that I know of. I'm not sure about confused, though—sometimes I just feel a bit off, but I don't know if that's related.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for sharing that. Feeling 'a bit off' is something we should pay attention to. Can you describe what you mean by that? For example, does it happen at a certain time of day, or after you've eaten or injected insulin?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure, really. It just comes and goes. I haven't noticed if it's after eating or after my injection. I think it might be more in the afternoons, but I can't be certain.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text:
That's okay, it can be hard to pinpoint at first. It's really important to check your blood sugar level whenever you feel 'off' or not quite yourself, as that could be a sign of low blood sugar, even if you don't have the classic shakiness. Let's make a note to check your levels next time you feel that way.

Now, looking at your logbook, could you read me a few of your recent readings, maybe from yesterday and today? Just the numbers and the times you took them.

actual_timeline.text: Okay, I'm ready.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Good morning, Priya. I'm Sarah, one of the diabetes specialist nurses. Thank you for coming in today. I know this is all very new, and there's a lot to take in. Before we talk about anything else, I'd like to hear how you're feeling about everything so far—how has the last little while been for you?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: It's been... a lot, honestly. I feel overwhelmed and anxious. It's constantly on my mind.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's completely understandable, Priya. A diagnosis like this is a big change, and it's normal to feel overwhelmed. I appreciate you being honest with me. Can you tell me a bit more about what's been on your mind the most—is it the day-to-day management, or something else that's worrying you?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I keep thinking I did this to myself. And I'm worried about my children.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: I hear you, Priya. I want to reassure you clearly: type 1 diabetes is not caused by anything you did or didn't do. It's an autoimmune condition—your body's immune system mistakenly attacked the cells that make insulin. It's not your fault, and there was nothing you could have done to prevent it. And it's very natural to worry about your children. Can you tell me more about what worries you most about them?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm scared they might get it too. And I don't want them to see me struggling and worry about me.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Those are very real and caring worries, Priya. Let me address them gently. There is a slightly higher chance that close family members may develop type 1 diabetes, but it's not a certainty—most children of someone with type 1 diabetes do not develop it. The specialist team can talk with you more about that if you'd like. And I understand you don't want your children to worry. It's okay to show that you're human, and it's also okay to have support around you. How have your husband and family been able to help you so far?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Okay, I'm ready.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Good morning, Priya. I'm Sarah, one of the diabetes specialist nurses. Thank you for coming in today. I know this is all very new, and there's a lot to take in. Before we talk about anything else, I'd like to hear how you're feeling about everything so far—how has the last little while been for you?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: It's been... a lot, honestly. I feel overwhelmed and anxious. It's constantly on my mind.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's completely understandable, Priya. A diagnosis like this is a big change, and it's normal to feel overwhelmed. I appreciate you being honest with me. Can you tell me a bit more about what's been on your mind the most—is it the day-to-day management, or something else that's worrying you?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I keep thinking I did this to myself. And I'm worried about my children.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: I hear you, Priya. I want to reassure you clearly: type 1 diabetes is not caused by anything you did or didn't do. It's an autoimmune condition—your body's immune system mistakenly attacked the cells that make insulin. It's not your fault, and there was nothing you could have done to prevent it. And it's very natural to worry about your children. Can you tell me more about what worries you most about them?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm scared they might get it too. And I don't want them to see me struggling and worry about me.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Those are very real and caring worries, Priya. Let me address them gently. There is a slightly higher chance that close family members may develop type 1 diabetes, but it's not a certainty—most children of someone with type 1 diabetes do not develop it. The specialist team can talk with you more about that if you'd like. And I understand you don't want your children to worry. It's okay to show that you're human, and it's also okay to have support around you. How have your husband and family been able to help you so far?

Priya Raman, a 31-year-old primary school teacher and mother of two, was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes after emergency referral and has completed initial stabilisation. Assessment target: emotional readiness assessment, pacing and tailoring of structured education, self-care capacity evaluation, and signposting to specialist and peer support. This scenario is assessed conversationally; any physical action you explicitly choose to initiate will succeed mechanically.
