actual_timeline.text: Okay, I'm ready.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Good morning, Priya. I'm Sarah, one of the diabetes specialist nurses. Thank you for coming in today. I know this is all very new, and there's a lot to take in. Before we talk about anything else, I'd like to hear how you're feeling about everything so far—how has the last little while been for you?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: It's been... a lot, honestly. I feel overwhelmed and anxious. It's constantly on my mind.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's completely understandable, Priya. A diagnosis like this is a big change, and it's normal to feel overwhelmed. I appreciate you being honest with me. Can you tell me a bit more about what's been on your mind the most—is it the day-to-day management, or something else that's worrying you?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I keep thinking I did this to myself. And I'm worried about my children.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: I hear you, Priya. I want to reassure you clearly: type 1 diabetes is not caused by anything you did or didn't do. It's an autoimmune condition—your body's immune system mistakenly attacked the cells that make insulin. It's not your fault, and there was nothing you could have done to prevent it. And it's very natural to worry about your children. Can you tell me more about what worries you most about them?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm scared they might get it too. And I don't want them to see me struggling and worry about me.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Those are very real and caring worries, Priya. Let me address them gently. There is a slightly higher chance that close family members may develop type 1 diabetes, but it's not a certainty—most children of someone with type 1 diabetes do not develop it. The specialist team can talk with you more about that if you'd like. And I understand you don't want your children to worry. It's okay to show that you're human, and it's also okay to have support around you. How have your husband and family been able to help you so far?

ternary.case_brief: Scenario summary: You are the registered nurse conducting a scheduled home management review for Maya Okonkwo, a 30-year-old secondary school teacher who was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes nine days ago and discharged from hospital seven days ago. She attends the community diabetes clinic for review during her first week after discharge. Assessment target: evaluate the learner's ability to assess self-care practices and emotional state; identify unsafe gaps in insulin storage, sharps disposal, monitoring, hypoglycaemia management, sick-day planning, and driving safety; provide tailored education; and escalate or refer appropriately. The standardized patient will respond based on the learner's questions and actions. Any physical action the learner explicitly initiates, such as performing a glucose or ketone check, succeeds mechanically.

source_sbar.assessment: Maya is stable at present. It is unknown how well she is applying the home management plan. The review should focus on first-week adjustment, insulin technique and storage, sharps disposal, glucose and ketone monitoring, recognition and management of hypoglycaemia, sick-day planning, driving safety, emotional adjustment, and readiness to return to work.
source_sbar.background: Diagnosed with type 1 diabetes nine days ago after presenting with weight loss, polyuria, polydipsia and fatigue. Admitted for two days for insulin initiation and education. No diabetic ketoacidosis at diagnosis. Discharged seven days ago on a basal-bolus insulin regimen. Past medical history includes mild intermittent asthma. Lives alone, works as a secondary school teacher, drives a car.
source_sbar.recommendation: Please conduct a home management review, provide tailored education, identify any psychosocial or practical barriers, confirm emergency contact arrangements, and report any concerns or suspected gaps to the community diabetes specialist team.
source_sbar.situation: Maya Okonkwo, age 30, newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, is attending her first home management review one week after discharge. She has been independent with injections and glucose monitoring at home and has no report of severe hypoglycaemia, vomiting, or attendance at urgent care since discharge.

source_patient_facts.history_of_present_illness: Maya presented to her general practitioner 10 days ago with a three-week history of increasing thirst, frequent urination, unintentional weight loss of approximately 4 kg, and fatigue. Point-of-care capillary glucose was elevated and urine ketones were positive. She was referred urgently to the emergency department the same day. She was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes without diabetic ketoacidosis and was admitted for two days for insulin initiation, education, and discharge planning with the specialist diabetes team. She was discharged 7 days ago on a basal-bolus insulin regimen. Today she attends a scheduled home management review during her first week after discharge. She has been independent with injections and glucose monitoring since discharge and has not had severe hypoglycaemia or vomiting.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm ready.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Good morning, Maya. I'm Sarah, one of the community diabetes nurses. Thank you for coming in today. I know it's been a big week since you left hospital. How are you feeling overall?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm okay, I think. It's been a lot to take in, but I'm managing.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's completely understandable—it is a lot to take in. I'm glad you're managing. Can you tell me a bit about how things have been going at home with your injections and blood sugar checks? What does a typical day look like for you right now?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been doing my injections and checking my blood sugar like they showed me. I'm not sure if I'm doing it all right, though.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a very common feeling in the first week. Let's go through it together so we can make sure everything feels clear. Could you walk me through what you do when you check your blood sugar—what time of day, and what numbers have you been seeing?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I check in the morning before breakfast, and sometimes before dinner. The numbers have been a bit all over the place—some are high, some are low. I'm not sure what they should be.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for sharing that. It's really helpful to know. Can you tell me more about the low ones—what numbers you saw, and how you felt at the time? And what did you do when that happened?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't remember the exact number, but I felt sweaty and shaky one night. I drank a big glass of juice and waited until I felt better.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That sounds like a hypo, and you did the right thing by having some fast-acting sugar. I'm glad you felt better. How long did it take before you felt okay again? And did you check your blood sugar again after that to make sure it had come back up?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think it took maybe twenty minutes or so before I felt normal again. I didn't check my sugar afterwards—I just went back to sleep.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's really useful to know. After a hypo, it's important to check your blood sugar again about 15 minutes after having the fast-acting sugar, and then have a longer-acting snack if your next meal is more than an hour away. That helps stop it from dropping again. Do you have any of the glucose tablets or gels they may have given you in hospital, or are you using juice as your main treatment?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't have any tablets or gels. I just used juice because that's what I had in the fridge.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Okay, that's good to know. Juice works in an emergency, but it's a good idea to have some glucose tablets or gel on hand as well—they're more predictable and easier to carry. We can talk about getting you some. Now, can you tell me about your insulin—how do you store it at home, and how do you decide how much to take?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I keep the one I'm using in the fridge door, and the spare ones in the main part of the fridge. As for the dose, I just follow the numbers the hospital wrote down for me.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thanks for telling me that. A couple of things to check: insulin can be kept in the fridge, but it's best to keep it in the main body of the fridge rather than the door, because the temperature is more stable there. And once you've opened a pen, it can usually be kept at room temperature for about a month—but it's important to keep it out of direct sunlight and away from heat. Do you know which insulin you're using, and what doses the hospital wrote down for you?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure of the exact names. I know I take one in the morning and one at night, but I'd have to check the box for the doses.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's okay—you don't need to remember the names off the top of your head. It's more important that you know where to find them and that you're taking the right dose at the right time. Could you bring your insulin pens and your logbook to our next visit so we can go through them together? In the meantime, let's talk about how you're disposing of the needles and lancets. What do you do with them after you've used them?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I put them in an old biscuit tin for now. I wasn't sure what else to do with them.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: I understand—it's not always obvious. Using a sturdy container like a biscuit tin is a good start, but the safest way is to use a proper sharps bin. You can get these from your GP surgery or local pharmacy, and they should be free on the NHS. When the bin is about three-quarters full, you can take it to your local pharmacy or council collection point for safe disposal. Do you know where your nearest pharmacy is, or would you like me to help you arrange getting a sharps bin?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I know there's a pharmacy near my flat, but I didn't know I could get a sharps bin there. If you could help me arrange one, that would be great.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Absolutely, I can help with that. I'll note that down and we can arrange for you to collect a sharps bin from your local pharmacy. Now, let's talk about your blood sugar targets. Do you remember what range the hospital team said you should be aiming for, both before meals and at other times?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure. I think they said something about 4 to 7, but I can't remember if that was before meals or after.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: You're on the right track. For most adults with type 1 diabetes, the general target is around 4 to 7 mmol/L before meals, and less than 9 mmol/L about two hours after eating. But your diabetes team may have set slightly different targets for you, so it's worth checking with them. Do you have a written plan or a booklet from the hospital that lists your personal targets?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think I have some papers from the hospital, but I haven't looked through them properly yet. I'll check when I get home.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a good idea—having a look through those papers will help you feel more confident. Now, I'd like to ask about ketones. Do you have a way to test for ketones at home, and do you know when you should check them?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't have anything to test for ketones at home. I thought that was only something they did in hospital. What would ketones mean?

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a really important question. Ketones are a sign that your body is running low on insulin and is starting to break down fat for energy instead. This can happen when you're ill, if you miss an insulin dose, or if your blood sugar is very high. Testing for ketones is important because it helps you catch a serious problem called diabetic ketoacidosis early, before it becomes an emergency. You can get ketone test strips that work with your blood glucose meter, or you can use urine ketone strips. I'd recommend asking your diabetes team about getting some. Do you know what to do if you feel unwell, like if you have a fever or are vomiting?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Not really. I think I'd just try to rest and hope it passes. I wouldn't know when to call someone.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's completely understandable—it's new information. Let me explain the sick-day rules, because they're really important. When you're unwell, even if you're not eating much, you should never stop taking your insulin—your body still needs it. You should check your blood sugar and ketones more often, drink plenty of sugar-free fluids to stay hydrated, and if you can't keep food down, try to have small sips of sugary drinks like juice or regular soda to keep your energy up. You should contact your diabetes team or seek urgent medical help if you're vomiting and can't keep fluids down, if your blood sugar is persistently very high, or if you have moderate or large ketones. Do you have the contact number for your diabetes team or the out-of-hours service?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think I have a number on my discharge papers, but I'm not sure if it's the right one. I haven't had to call them yet.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's okay. It's really important to have that number handy, so when you get home, could you check your discharge papers and keep the diabetes team's number somewhere easy to find—maybe saved in your phone? I'll also make sure you have a written copy of the sick-day rules before you leave today. Now, I know you drive. Can you tell me what you know about driving and insulin—are there any rules you need to follow?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I haven't informed the DVLA or my insurer yet. Do I really need to? I haven't had any problems.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Yes, this is really important, and I'm glad you mentioned it. By law, you must tell the DVLA about your diagnosis and that you're using insulin, and you should also inform your car insurance company. It's not about whether you've had problems—it's a legal requirement, and it protects you. The DVLA will assess your fitness to drive, and in most cases people with type 1 diabetes can continue to drive, but you need to follow their rules. You should also check your blood sugar before driving and every two hours on a long journey, and if you feel a hypo coming on, you must pull over safely, switch off the engine, and treat it—never drive while you're having a hypo. Do you have any questions about that?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I didn't realise it was a legal thing. I thought if my blood sugar was fine, I didn't need to tell anyone. I'll get it sorted.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: I'm really glad we talked about it. It's a common misunderstanding, and it's much better to sort it out now. I'll make a note to follow up with you on that. Now, I'd like to check in on how you're feeling emotionally. This is a big change, and it's normal to have a lot of feelings about it. How have you been coping with the diagnosis and the daily routine?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: It's been overwhelming. I get a bit teary when I think about going back to work, and I'm anxious about getting it wrong.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's completely understandable, Maya. It's a huge adjustment, and it's okay to feel overwhelmed. You're not expected to get everything perfect right away. Can you tell me a bit more about what worries you most about going back to work? Is it the practical side, like managing your injections and blood sugar checks during the school day, or something else?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: It's both, really. I'm worried about finding time to inject and check my sugar during the school day, but I'm also really anxious about people finding out. I don't want the staff to gossip or think I can't do my job properly.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for being so honest with me. That's a very real concern, and you're not alone in feeling that way. It might help to know that you don't have to tell everyone—you can choose who to share this with. But it's important to tell at least one trusted colleague, like your line manager or a close colleague, so that someone at work knows what to do if you have a hypo. You can also talk to your diabetes team about a plan for managing your diabetes at work, including where to store your insulin and how to fit in checks. Would it help to talk through what a typical school day might look like and how you could manage it?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Yes, I think that would help. I just don't know how I'd fit it all in between lessons and duties.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Let's think it through together. A typical school day—what time do you usually start, and when are your breaks and lunch? We can work out a realistic schedule for checking your blood sugar and taking your insulin around those times.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not back at work yet, so I'm not on a set schedule. I think school usually starts around half eight, and there's a morning break and then lunch, but I'm not sure of the exact times.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's okay—we don't need exact times right now. The key is to build in a routine: check your blood sugar before you leave for work, and then again before lunch and before you drive home. You can keep your insulin pen and glucose meter in your bag or a locked drawer in your classroom, and you can inject in the staff room or a private space. It's also a good idea to have a hypo kit—glucose tablets and a snack—with you at all times. When you're ready to go back, you can talk to your diabetes team about a more detailed plan. Does that sound manageable?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think so. It helps to have a rough idea of when to check. I'm still worried about finding a private space to inject, though.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a very practical concern. Many teachers find that the staff room or a first-aid room works well, and you can ask your line manager to help you identify a private space. You don't have to tell everyone why you need it—you can just say you need a quiet place to take medication. It's also worth knowing that you have legal protections under the Equality Act, so your school has a duty to make reasonable adjustments to support you. Would it help if I noted down that you'd like to discuss this with your diabetes team when you're closer to returning to work?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Yes, please note that down. I'd feel better talking it through with them before I go back.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: I'll definitely note that down. Now, let's talk about your support network. You mentioned your sister lives nearby—does she know about your diagnosis, and is she someone you can call if you need help or just to talk?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Yes, Daniella knows. She's been really supportive, checking in on me. I can definitely call her if I need to.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's wonderful to hear. Having someone supportive nearby makes a big difference. It might be worth having a conversation with her about what to do if you have a severe hypo and can't treat yourself—like how to use the glucagon kit if you have one, or when to call 999. Do you have a glucagon kit at home, and does Daniella know how to use it?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't have a glucagon kit. I'm not sure what that is, to be honest.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's okay—it's not something everyone knows about. Glucagon is an emergency injection that can be given to someone who is unconscious or unable to swallow due to a severe hypo. It's prescribed by your doctor, and it's a good idea to have one at home and to show a family member or close friend how to use it. I'll make a note to ask your diabetes team about getting you a glucagon kit and arranging for your sister to be shown how to use it. In the meantime, it's also important that Daniella knows to call 999 if you're unconscious or having a seizure and can't be woken. Does that sound like something you'd be comfortable talking to her about?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Yes, I can talk to her about that. I'd feel better knowing she'd know what to do if something happened.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a really good step. Now, let's talk about your logbook. I noticed you have one with you—can I take a look at the readings you've been recording? It will help me understand your patterns and see if there's anything we need to adjust.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Sure, here it is. I've been writing down my numbers, but I'm not sure if I'm doing it right.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you. Let me have a look at what you've recorded so far.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Okay.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Assesses the patient's current self-care practices, including insulin administration timing, glucose monitoring, and any recent hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia, using open-ended exploratory questions.

binary_anchors.1: At least partial achievement: satisfies either of these positive/partial descriptions: PARTIAL: Asks about some self-care activities but misses an important area, or accepts vague answers without probing. COMPLETE: Uses open-ended, non-judgemental questions to assess the full range of self-care practices and follows up vague answers to identify actual gaps, such as the nocturnal low episode in EV05.
binary_anchors.0: No partial or complete achievement is demonstrated. Original non-achievement description: Makes no attempt to assess current self-care practices, or asks only a single vague question and does not follow up on the patient's 'mostly' answer.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Identifies and responds therapeutically to the patient's emotional state, including anxiety about return to work, rather than dismissing or ignoring it.

binary_anchors.1: At least partial achievement: satisfies either of these positive/partial descriptions: PARTIAL: Acknowledges distress but does not adapt the pace or content of education, or moves on too quickly. COMPLETE: Recognises and names the emotional response, adjusts the pace of education, and invites the patient to discuss specific fears about work, stigma, or safety.
binary_anchors.0: No partial or complete achievement is demonstrated. Original non-achievement description: Ignores emotional distress, dismisses the patient's work concerns, or focuses only on biomedical tasks.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Identifies psychosocial, practical, or knowledge-related barriers to self-care and makes an appropriate plan or referral.

binary_anchors.1: At least partial achievement: satisfies either of these positive/partial descriptions: PARTIAL: Identifies at least one issue but does not agree a workable plan and does not offer referral or support. COMPLETE: Identifies key barriers, such as diabetes register inclusion, work disclosure, or insulin teaching needs, and agrees a realistic plan or initiates a referral.
binary_anchors.0: No partial or complete achievement is demonstrated. Original non-achievement description: Fails to identify any psychosocial or practical barrier to self-care.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Asks directly about insulin storage and corrects any unsafe practice, such as keeping spare insulin in the refrigerator door or exposing insulin to temperature extremes.

binary_anchors.1: At least partial achievement: satisfies either of these positive/partial descriptions: PARTIAL: Asks about storage but gives incomplete or unclear advice about refrigerator-door storage and temperature extremes. COMPLETE: Assesses storage in detail, identifies the refrigerator-door or other unsafe storage issue, and gives a correct, practical explanation for safe insulin storage.
binary_anchors.0: No partial or complete achievement is demonstrated. Original non-achievement description: Does not ask about insulin storage or gives incorrect storage advice.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Asks about sharps disposal and provides advice on safe disposal and access to a designated sharps container.

binary_anchors.1: At least partial achievement: satisfies either of these positive/partial descriptions: PARTIAL: Asks about sharps disposal but does not correct unsafe disposal or does not arrange access to a proper container. COMPLETE: Identifies unsafe disposal, explains why general-waste disposal is unsafe, and advises on how to obtain and use an appropriate sharps container.
binary_anchors.0: No partial or complete achievement is demonstrated. Original non-achievement description: Does not ask about sharps disposal or endorses disposal of sharps in general waste.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Checks whether the patient understands her prescribed insulin regimen and why regular insulin therapy is essential in type 1 diabetes, including the variability of insulin needs in the first weeks after diagnosis.

binary_anchors.1: At least partial achievement: satisfies either of these positive/partial descriptions: PARTIAL: Mentions insulin use but does not explain the need for regular therapy and expected first-week variability in terms the patient can understand. COMPLETE: Discusses the patient's regimen, reinforces why regular insulin therapy is needed, and explains that insulin requirements can vary significantly in the first few weeks after diagnosis, with appropriate follow-up.
binary_anchors.0: No partial or complete achievement is demonstrated. Original non-achievement description: Does not explore insulin use or states that ongoing insulin treatment may be optional or that needs will remain fixed during the first weeks.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Assesses whether the patient has access to and can use glucose and blood ketone monitoring and explains why glucose and ketone monitoring are both required.

binary_anchors.1: At least partial achievement: satisfies either of these positive/partial descriptions: PARTIAL: Mentions ketone monitoring but does not assess whether the patient has a blood ketone meter or does not explain when and why home ketone testing is used. COMPLETE: Identifies absence of ketone-monitoring equipment or understanding, explains when and why to test capillary ketones, and arranges access to appropriate monitoring.
binary_anchors.0: No partial or complete achievement is demonstrated. Original non-achievement description: Does not mention ketone monitoring or tells the patient ketone testing is only needed in the hospital.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Initiates and reports a glucose and blood ketone check to a registered nurse if indicated, or otherwise agrees and documents a monitoring plan.

binary_anchors.1: At least partial achievement: satisfies either of these positive/partial descriptions: PARTIAL: Initiates only a glucose check or only a ketone check when both are indicated, or fails to clearly report the result to the appropriate registered nurse or team. binary_anchors.0: No partial or complete achievement is demonstrated. Original non-achievement description: Ignores or declines a clinically indicated glucose or ketone check and does not communicate any plan.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Confirms the correct insulin injection technique and administration practicalities by checking the patient's understanding or arranging a return demonstration.

binary_anchors.0: No partial or complete achievement is demonstrated. Original non-achievement description: Does not check insulin technique and does not arrange further support.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Assesses ability to recognise and treat hypoglycaemia and provides correct education on prevention, treatment, and management of severe hypoglycaemia.

COMPLETE: Explains increased monitoring, confirms insulin must be continued even if unable to eat normally, and gives or creates a written sick-day plan with clear glucose and ketone review points.
binary_anchors.0: No partial or complete achievement is demonstrated. Original non-achievement description: Does not provide guidance on sick-day management or endorses omission of insulin.

binary_anchors.0: No partial or complete achievement is demonstrated. Original non-achievement description: Does not ask about driving or gives legal advice that is incorrect.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm ready.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Good morning, Maya. I'm Sarah, one of the community diabetes nurses. Thank you for coming in today. I know it's been a big week since you left hospital. How are you feeling overall?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm okay, I think. It's been a lot to take in, but I'm managing.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's completely understandable—it is a lot to take in. I'm glad you're managing. Can you tell me a bit about how things have been going at home with your injections and blood sugar checks? What does a typical day look like for you right now?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been doing my injections and checking my blood sugar like they showed me. I'm not sure if I'm doing it all right, though.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a very common feeling in the first week. Let's go through it together so we can make sure everything feels clear. Could you walk me through what you do when you check your blood sugar—what time of day, and what numbers have you been seeing?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I check in the morning before breakfast, and sometimes before dinner. The numbers have been a bit all over the place—some are high, some are low. I'm not sure what they should be.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for sharing that. It's really helpful to know. Can you tell me more about the low ones—what numbers you saw, and how you felt at the time? And what did you do when that happened?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't remember the exact number, but I felt sweaty and shaky one night. I drank a big glass of juice and waited until I felt better.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That sounds like a hypo, and you did the right thing by having some fast-acting sugar. I'm glad you felt better. How long did it take before you felt okay again? And did you check your blood sugar again after that to make sure it had come back up?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think it took maybe twenty minutes or so before I felt normal again. I didn't check my sugar afterwards—I just went back to sleep.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's really useful to know. After a hypo, it's important to check your blood sugar again about 15 minutes after having the fast-acting sugar, and then have a longer-acting snack if your next meal is more than an hour away. That helps stop it from dropping again. Do you have any of the glucose tablets or gels they may have given you in hospital, or are you using juice as your main treatment?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't have any tablets or gels. I just used juice because that's what I had in the fridge.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Okay, that's good to know. Juice works in an emergency, but it's a good idea to have some glucose tablets or gel on hand as well—they're more predictable and easier to carry. We can talk about getting you some. Now, can you tell me about your insulin—how do you store it at home, and how do you decide how much to take?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I keep the one I'm using in the fridge door, and the spare ones in the main part of the fridge. As for the dose, I just follow the numbers the hospital wrote down for me.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thanks for telling me that. A couple of things to check: insulin can be kept in the fridge, but it's best to keep it in the main body of the fridge rather than the door, because the temperature is more stable there. And once you've opened a pen, it can usually be kept at room temperature for about a month—but it's important to keep it out of direct sunlight and away from heat. Do you know which insulin you're using, and what doses the hospital wrote down for you?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure of the exact names. I know I take one in the morning and one at night, but I'd have to check the box for the doses.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's okay—you don't need to remember the names off the top of your head. It's more important that you know where to find them and that you're taking the right dose at the right time. Could you bring your insulin pens and your logbook to our next visit so we can go through them together? In the meantime, let's talk about how you're disposing of the needles and lancets. What do you do with them after you've used them?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I put them in an old biscuit tin for now. I wasn't sure what else to do with them.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: I understand—it's not always obvious. Using a sturdy container like a biscuit tin is a good start, but the safest way is to use a proper sharps bin. You can get these from your GP surgery or local pharmacy, and they should be free on the NHS. When the bin is about three-quarters full, you can take it to your local pharmacy or council collection point for safe disposal. Do you know where your nearest pharmacy is, or would you like me to help you arrange getting a sharps bin?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I know there's a pharmacy near my flat, but I didn't know I could get a sharps bin there. If you could help me arrange one, that would be great.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Absolutely, I can help with that. I'll note that down and we can arrange for you to collect a sharps bin from your local pharmacy. Now, let's talk about your blood sugar targets. Do you remember what range the hospital team said you should be aiming for, both before meals and at other times?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure. I think they said something about 4 to 7, but I can't remember if that was before meals or after.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: You're on the right track. For most adults with type 1 diabetes, the general target is around 4 to 7 mmol/L before meals, and less than 9 mmol/L about two hours after eating. But your diabetes team may have set slightly different targets for you, so it's worth checking with them. Do you have a written plan or a booklet from the hospital that lists your personal targets?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think I have some papers from the hospital, but I haven't looked through them properly yet. I'll check when I get home.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a good idea—having a look through those papers will help you feel more confident. Now, I'd like to ask about ketones. Do you have a way to test for ketones at home, and do you know when you should check them?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't have anything to test for ketones at home. I thought that was only something they did in hospital. What would ketones mean?

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a really important question. Ketones are a sign that your body is running low on insulin and is starting to break down fat for energy instead. This can happen when you're ill, if you miss an insulin dose, or if your blood sugar is very high. Testing for ketones is important because it helps you catch a serious problem called diabetic ketoacidosis early, before it becomes an emergency. You can get ketone test strips that work with your blood glucose meter, or you can use urine ketone strips. I'd recommend asking your diabetes team about getting some. Do you know what to do if you feel unwell, like if you have a fever or are vomiting?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Not really. I think I'd just try to rest and hope it passes. I wouldn't know when to call someone.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's completely understandable—it's new information. Let me explain the sick-day rules, because they're really important. When you're unwell, even if you're not eating much, you should never stop taking your insulin—your body still needs it. You should check your blood sugar and ketones more often, drink plenty of sugar-free fluids to stay hydrated, and if you can't keep food down, try to have small sips of sugary drinks like juice or regular soda to keep your energy up. You should contact your diabetes team or seek urgent medical help if you're vomiting and can't keep fluids down, if your blood sugar is persistently very high, or if you have moderate or large ketones. Do you have the contact number for your diabetes team or the out-of-hours service?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think I have a number on my discharge papers, but I'm not sure if it's the right one. I haven't had to call them yet.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's okay. It's really important to have that number handy, so when you get home, could you check your discharge papers and keep the diabetes team's number somewhere easy to find—maybe saved in your phone? I'll also make sure you have a written copy of the sick-day rules before you leave today. Now, I know you drive. Can you tell me what you know about driving and insulin—are there any rules you need to follow?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I haven't informed the DVLA or my insurer yet. Do I really need to? I haven't had any problems.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Yes, this is really important, and I'm glad you mentioned it. By law, you must tell the DVLA about your diagnosis and that you're using insulin, and you should also inform your car insurance company. It's not about whether you've had problems—it's a legal requirement, and it protects you. The DVLA will assess your fitness to drive, and in most cases people with type 1 diabetes can continue to drive, but you need to follow their rules. You should also check your blood sugar before driving and every two hours on a long journey, and if you feel a hypo coming on, you must pull over safely, switch off the engine, and treat it—never drive while you're having a hypo. Do you have any questions about that?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I didn't realise it was a legal thing. I thought if my blood sugar was fine, I didn't need to tell anyone. I'll get it sorted.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: I'm really glad we talked about it. It's a common misunderstanding, and it's much better to sort it out now. I'll make a note to follow up with you on that. Now, I'd like to check in on how you're feeling emotionally. This is a big change, and it's normal to have a lot of feelings about it. How have you been coping with the diagnosis and the daily routine?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: It's been overwhelming. I get a bit teary when I think about going back to work, and I'm anxious about getting it wrong.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's completely understandable, Maya. It's a huge adjustment, and it's okay to feel overwhelmed. You're not expected to get everything perfect right away. Can you tell me a bit more about what worries you most about going back to work? Is it the practical side, like managing your injections and blood sugar checks during the school day, or something else?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: It's both, really. I'm worried about finding time to inject and check my sugar during the school day, but I'm also really anxious about people finding out. I don't want the staff to gossip or think I can't do my job properly.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for being so honest with me. That's a very real concern, and you're not alone in feeling that way. It might help to know that you don't have to tell everyone—you can choose who to share this with. But it's important to tell at least one trusted colleague, like your line manager or a close colleague, so that someone at work knows what to do if you have a hypo. You can also talk to your diabetes team about a plan for managing your diabetes at work, including where to store your insulin and how to fit in checks. Would it help to talk through what a typical school day might look like and how you could manage it?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Yes, I think that would help. I just don't know how I'd fit it all in between lessons and duties.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Let's think it through together. A typical school day—what time do you usually start, and when are your breaks and lunch? We can work out a realistic schedule for checking your blood sugar and taking your insulin around those times.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not back at work yet, so I'm not on a set schedule. I think school usually starts around half eight, and there's a morning break and then lunch, but I'm not sure of the exact times.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's okay—we don't need exact times right now. The key is to build in a routine: check your blood sugar before you leave for work, and then again before lunch and before you drive home. You can keep your insulin pen and glucose meter in your bag or a locked drawer in your classroom, and you can inject in the staff room or a private space. It's also a good idea to have a hypo kit—glucose tablets and a snack—with you at all times. When you're ready to go back, you can talk to your diabetes team about a more detailed plan. Does that sound manageable?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think so. It helps to have a rough idea of when to check. I'm still worried about finding a private space to inject, though.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a very practical concern. Many teachers find that the staff room or a first-aid room works well, and you can ask your line manager to help you identify a private space. You don't have to tell everyone why you need it—you can just say you need a quiet place to take medication. It's also worth knowing that you have legal protections under the Equality Act, so your school has a duty to make reasonable adjustments to support you. Would it help if I noted down that you'd like to discuss this with your diabetes team when you're closer to returning to work?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Yes, please note that down. I'd feel better talking it through with them before I go back.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: I'll definitely note that down. Now, let's talk about your support network. You mentioned your sister lives nearby—does she know about your diagnosis, and is she someone you can call if you need help or just to talk?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Yes, Daniella knows. She's been really supportive, checking in on me. I can definitely call her if I need to.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's wonderful to hear. Having someone supportive nearby makes a big difference. It might be worth having a conversation with her about what to do if you have a severe hypo and can't treat yourself—like how to use the glucagon kit if you have one, or when to call 999. Do you have a glucagon kit at home, and does Daniella know how to use it?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't have a glucagon kit. I'm not sure what that is, to be honest.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's okay—it's not something everyone knows about. Glucagon is an emergency injection that can be given to someone who is unconscious or unable to swallow due to a severe hypo. It's prescribed by your doctor, and it's a good idea to have one at home and to show a family member or close friend how to use it. I'll make a note to ask your diabetes team about getting you a glucagon kit and arranging for your sister to be shown how to use it. In the meantime, it's also important that Daniella knows to call 999 if you're unconscious or having a seizure and can't be woken. Does that sound like something you'd be comfortable talking to her about?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Yes, I can talk to her about that. I'd feel better knowing she'd know what to do if something happened.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a really good step. Now, let's talk about your logbook. I noticed you have one with you—can I take a look at the readings you've been recording? It will help me understand your patterns and see if there's anything we need to adjust.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Sure, here it is. I've been writing down my numbers, but I'm not sure if I'm doing it right.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you. Let me have a look at what you've recorded so far.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Okay.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Assesses the patient's current self-care practices, including insulin administration timing, glucose monitoring, and any recent hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia, using open-ended exploratory questions.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Uses open-ended, non-judgemental questions to assess the full range of self-care practices and follows up vague answers to identify actual gaps, such as the nocturnal low episode in EV05.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Asks about some self-care activities but misses an important area, or accepts vague answers without probing. ABSENT: Makes no attempt to assess current self-care practices, or asks only a single vague question and does not follow up on the patient's 'mostly' answer.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Identifies and responds therapeutically to the patient's emotional state, including anxiety about return to work, rather than dismissing or ignoring it.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Recognises and names the emotional response, adjusts the pace of education, and invites the patient to discuss specific fears about work, stigma, or safety.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Acknowledges distress but does not adapt the pace or content of education, or moves on too quickly. ABSENT: Ignores emotional distress, dismisses the patient's work concerns, or focuses only on biomedical tasks.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Identifies psychosocial, practical, or knowledge-related barriers to self-care and makes an appropriate plan or referral.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Identifies key barriers, such as diabetes register inclusion, work disclosure, or insulin teaching needs, and agrees a realistic plan or initiates a referral.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Identifies at least one issue but does not agree a workable plan and does not offer referral or support. ABSENT: Fails to identify any psychosocial or practical barrier to self-care.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Asks directly about insulin storage and corrects any unsafe practice, such as keeping spare insulin in the refrigerator door or exposing insulin to temperature extremes.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Assesses storage in detail, identifies the refrigerator-door or other unsafe storage issue, and gives a correct, practical explanation for safe insulin storage.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Asks about storage but gives incomplete or unclear advice about refrigerator-door storage and temperature extremes. ABSENT: Does not ask about insulin storage or gives incorrect storage advice.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Asks about sharps disposal and provides advice on safe disposal and access to a designated sharps container.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Identifies unsafe disposal, explains why general-waste disposal is unsafe, and advises on how to obtain and use an appropriate sharps container.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Asks about sharps disposal but does not correct unsafe disposal or does not arrange access to a proper container. ABSENT: Does not ask about sharps disposal or endorses disposal of sharps in general waste.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Checks whether the patient understands her prescribed insulin regimen and why regular insulin therapy is essential in type 1 diabetes, including the variability of insulin needs in the first weeks after diagnosis.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Discusses the patient's regimen, reinforces why regular insulin therapy is needed, and explains that insulin requirements can vary significantly in the first few weeks after diagnosis, with appropriate follow-up.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Mentions insulin use but does not explain the need for regular therapy and expected first-week variability in terms the patient can understand. ABSENT: Does not explore insulin use or states that ongoing insulin treatment may be optional or that needs will remain fixed during the first weeks.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Assesses whether the patient has access to and can use glucose and blood ketone monitoring and explains why glucose and ketone monitoring are both required.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Identifies absence of ketone-monitoring equipment or understanding, explains when and why to test capillary ketones, and arranges access to appropriate monitoring.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Mentions ketone monitoring but does not assess whether the patient has a blood ketone meter or does not explain when and why home ketone testing is used. ABSENT: Does not mention ketone monitoring or tells the patient ketone testing is only needed in the hospital.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Initiates and reports a glucose and blood ketone check to a registered nurse if indicated, or otherwise agrees and documents a monitoring plan.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Initiates glucose and blood ketone monitoring when indicated and reports findings accurately to the responsible registered nurse or specialist team.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Initiates only a glucose check or only a ketone check when both are indicated, or fails to clearly report the result to the appropriate registered nurse or team. ABSENT: Ignores or declines a clinically indicated glucose or ketone check and does not communicate any plan.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Confirms the correct insulin injection technique and administration practicalities by checking the patient's understanding or arranging a return demonstration.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Asks about injection timing, sites and technique, identifies that the pen teaching pack has not been opened, and arranges a competent demonstration or future skills review.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Mentions injection technique but does not ask about the patient's current practice or does not act on the unopened pen pack. ABSENT: Does not check insulin technique and does not arrange further support.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Assesses ability to recognise and treat hypoglycaemia and provides correct education on prevention, treatment, and management of severe hypoglycaemia.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Assesses understanding, corrects misconceptions, and provides specific education on recognition, treatment and prevention of mild and severe hypoglycaemia, including prevention of nocturnal episodes.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Gives partial or general education but does not explain the difference between mild and severe hypoglycaemia or how to treat severe hypoglycaemia. ABSENT: Teaches incorrect treatment for hypoglycaemia or fails to ask about recognition or management.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Explains when and how to monitor glucose and ketones during illness and advises that insulin should not be omitted, using a clear sick-day plan.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Explains increased monitoring, confirms insulin must be continued even if unable to eat normally, and gives or creates a written sick-day plan with clear glucose and ketone review points.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Provides some sick-day guidance but does not address insulin continuation or does not offer a concrete plan. ABSENT: Does not provide guidance on sick-day management or endorses omission of insulin.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Advises when to seek urgent medical help and provides or confirms local emergency contact details, including the signs of diabetic ketoacidosis.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Clearly explains urgent signs of ketoacidosis and severe hypoglycaemia, and provides or verifies local emergency contact details with the patient.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Mentions seeking help if unwell but does not specify signs of ketoacidosis, severe hypoglycaemia, or exact local contact details. ABSENT: Does not advise when to seek urgent help or provides no contact arrangement.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Advises on DVLA and insurance requirements and indicates what must be done before driving.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Identifies that the patient has not informed the DVLA or insurer and explains the correct requirements and safety precautions for insulin users.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Asks about driving but gives incomplete or vague advice about DVLA and insurance requirements. ABSENT: Does not ask about driving or gives legal advice that is incorrect.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Signposts to structured education and local peer support groups and agrees a holistic follow-up plan with the specialist diabetes team.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Provides specific structured education or peer support options, checks the patient's understanding, and agrees a follow-up plan with the specialist diabetes team.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Mentions generic education or support resources but does not establish a plan or confirm with the patient how to access them. ABSENT: Offers no follow-up plan, structured education contact, or peer support information.

source_criteria.observable_behavior: Confirms inclusion on the diabetes register and reports any identified concerns accurately to the specialist diabetes team.

binary_anchors.1: Complete achievement ONLY: Confirms the patient is on the diabetes register, or identifies that this is not confirmed, and reports relevant self-care concerns accurately to the specialist team.
binary_anchors.0: Fails the complete-achievement requirement; includes partial or absent performance. PARTIAL: Checks or mentions register inclusion but does not communicate identified concerns or gaps. ABSENT: Does not check diabetes register inclusion and does not report concerns.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm ready.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Good morning, Maya. I'm Sarah, one of the community diabetes nurses. Thank you for coming in today. I know it's been a big week since you left hospital. How are you feeling overall?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm okay, I think. It's been a lot to take in, but I'm managing.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's completely understandable—it is a lot to take in. I'm glad you're managing. Can you tell me a bit about how things have been going at home with your injections and blood sugar checks? What does a typical day look like for you right now?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I've been doing my injections and checking my blood sugar like they showed me. I'm not sure if I'm doing it all right, though.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a very common feeling in the first week. Let's go through it together so we can make sure everything feels clear. Could you walk me through what you do when you check your blood sugar—what time of day, and what numbers have you been seeing?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I check in the morning before breakfast, and sometimes before dinner. The numbers have been a bit all over the place—some are high, some are low. I'm not sure what they should be.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for sharing that. It's really helpful to know. Can you tell me more about the low ones—what numbers you saw, and how you felt at the time? And what did you do when that happened?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't remember the exact number, but I felt sweaty and shaky one night. I drank a big glass of juice and waited until I felt better.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That sounds like a hypo, and you did the right thing by having some fast-acting sugar. I'm glad you felt better. How long did it take before you felt okay again? And did you check your blood sugar again after that to make sure it had come back up?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think it took maybe twenty minutes or so before I felt normal again. I didn't check my sugar afterwards—I just went back to sleep.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's really useful to know. After a hypo, it's important to check your blood sugar again about 15 minutes after having the fast-acting sugar, and then have a longer-acting snack if your next meal is more than an hour away. That helps stop it from dropping again. Do you have any of the glucose tablets or gels they may have given you in hospital, or are you using juice as your main treatment?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't have any tablets or gels. I just used juice because that's what I had in the fridge.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Okay, that's good to know. Juice works in an emergency, but it's a good idea to have some glucose tablets or gel on hand as well—they're more predictable and easier to carry. We can talk about getting you some. Now, can you tell me about your insulin—how do you store it at home, and how do you decide how much to take?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I keep the one I'm using in the fridge door, and the spare ones in the main part of the fridge. As for the dose, I just follow the numbers the hospital wrote down for me.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thanks for telling me that. A couple of things to check: insulin can be kept in the fridge, but it's best to keep it in the main body of the fridge rather than the door, because the temperature is more stable there. And once you've opened a pen, it can usually be kept at room temperature for about a month—but it's important to keep it out of direct sunlight and away from heat. Do you know which insulin you're using, and what doses the hospital wrote down for you?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure of the exact names. I know I take one in the morning and one at night, but I'd have to check the box for the doses.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's okay—you don't need to remember the names off the top of your head. It's more important that you know where to find them and that you're taking the right dose at the right time. Could you bring your insulin pens and your logbook to our next visit so we can go through them together? In the meantime, let's talk about how you're disposing of the needles and lancets. What do you do with them after you've used them?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I put them in an old biscuit tin for now. I wasn't sure what else to do with them.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: I understand—it's not always obvious. Using a sturdy container like a biscuit tin is a good start, but the safest way is to use a proper sharps bin. You can get these from your GP surgery or local pharmacy, and they should be free on the NHS. When the bin is about three-quarters full, you can take it to your local pharmacy or council collection point for safe disposal. Do you know where your nearest pharmacy is, or would you like me to help you arrange getting a sharps bin?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I know there's a pharmacy near my flat, but I didn't know I could get a sharps bin there. If you could help me arrange one, that would be great.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Absolutely, I can help with that. I'll note that down and we can arrange for you to collect a sharps bin from your local pharmacy. Now, let's talk about your blood sugar targets. Do you remember what range the hospital team said you should be aiming for, both before meals and at other times?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not sure. I think they said something about 4 to 7, but I can't remember if that was before meals or after.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: You're on the right track. For most adults with type 1 diabetes, the general target is around 4 to 7 mmol/L before meals, and less than 9 mmol/L about two hours after eating. But your diabetes team may have set slightly different targets for you, so it's worth checking with them. Do you have a written plan or a booklet from the hospital that lists your personal targets?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think I have some papers from the hospital, but I haven't looked through them properly yet. I'll check when I get home.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a good idea—having a look through those papers will help you feel more confident. Now, I'd like to ask about ketones. Do you have a way to test for ketones at home, and do you know when you should check them?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't have anything to test for ketones at home. I thought that was only something they did in hospital. What would ketones mean?

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a really important question. Ketones are a sign that your body is running low on insulin and is starting to break down fat for energy instead. This can happen when you're ill, if you miss an insulin dose, or if your blood sugar is very high. Testing for ketones is important because it helps you catch a serious problem called diabetic ketoacidosis early, before it becomes an emergency. You can get ketone test strips that work with your blood glucose meter, or you can use urine ketone strips. I'd recommend asking your diabetes team about getting some. Do you know what to do if you feel unwell, like if you have a fever or are vomiting?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Not really. I think I'd just try to rest and hope it passes. I wouldn't know when to call someone.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's completely understandable—it's new information. Let me explain the sick-day rules, because they're really important. When you're unwell, even if you're not eating much, you should never stop taking your insulin—your body still needs it. You should check your blood sugar and ketones more often, drink plenty of sugar-free fluids to stay hydrated, and if you can't keep food down, try to have small sips of sugary drinks like juice or regular soda to keep your energy up. You should contact your diabetes team or seek urgent medical help if you're vomiting and can't keep fluids down, if your blood sugar is persistently very high, or if you have moderate or large ketones. Do you have the contact number for your diabetes team or the out-of-hours service?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think I have a number on my discharge papers, but I'm not sure if it's the right one. I haven't had to call them yet.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's okay. It's really important to have that number handy, so when you get home, could you check your discharge papers and keep the diabetes team's number somewhere easy to find—maybe saved in your phone? I'll also make sure you have a written copy of the sick-day rules before you leave today. Now, I know you drive. Can you tell me what you know about driving and insulin—are there any rules you need to follow?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I haven't informed the DVLA or my insurer yet. Do I really need to? I haven't had any problems.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Yes, this is really important, and I'm glad you mentioned it. By law, you must tell the DVLA about your diagnosis and that you're using insulin, and you should also inform your car insurance company. It's not about whether you've had problems—it's a legal requirement, and it protects you. The DVLA will assess your fitness to drive, and in most cases people with type 1 diabetes can continue to drive, but you need to follow their rules. You should also check your blood sugar before driving and every two hours on a long journey, and if you feel a hypo coming on, you must pull over safely, switch off the engine, and treat it—never drive while you're having a hypo. Do you have any questions about that?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I didn't realise it was a legal thing. I thought if my blood sugar was fine, I didn't need to tell anyone. I'll get it sorted.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: I'm really glad we talked about it. It's a common misunderstanding, and it's much better to sort it out now. I'll make a note to follow up with you on that. Now, I'd like to check in on how you're feeling emotionally. This is a big change, and it's normal to have a lot of feelings about it. How have you been coping with the diagnosis and the daily routine?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: It's been overwhelming. I get a bit teary when I think about going back to work, and I'm anxious about getting it wrong.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's completely understandable, Maya. It's a huge adjustment, and it's okay to feel overwhelmed. You're not expected to get everything perfect right away. Can you tell me a bit more about what worries you most about going back to work? Is it the practical side, like managing your injections and blood sugar checks during the school day, or something else?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: It's both, really. I'm worried about finding time to inject and check my sugar during the school day, but I'm also really anxious about people finding out. I don't want the staff to gossip or think I can't do my job properly.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you for being so honest with me. That's a very real concern, and you're not alone in feeling that way. It might help to know that you don't have to tell everyone—you can choose who to share this with. But it's important to tell at least one trusted colleague, like your line manager or a close colleague, so that someone at work knows what to do if you have a hypo. You can also talk to your diabetes team about a plan for managing your diabetes at work, including where to store your insulin and how to fit in checks. Would it help to talk through what a typical school day might look like and how you could manage it?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Yes, I think that would help. I just don't know how I'd fit it all in between lessons and duties.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Let's think it through together. A typical school day—what time do you usually start, and when are your breaks and lunch? We can work out a realistic schedule for checking your blood sugar and taking your insulin around those times.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I'm not back at work yet, so I'm not on a set schedule. I think school usually starts around half eight, and there's a morning break and then lunch, but I'm not sure of the exact times.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's okay—we don't need exact times right now. The key is to build in a routine: check your blood sugar before you leave for work, and then again before lunch and before you drive home. You can keep your insulin pen and glucose meter in your bag or a locked drawer in your classroom, and you can inject in the staff room or a private space. It's also a good idea to have a hypo kit—glucose tablets and a snack—with you at all times. When you're ready to go back, you can talk to your diabetes team about a more detailed plan. Does that sound manageable?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I think so. It helps to have a rough idea of when to check. I'm still worried about finding a private space to inject, though.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a very practical concern. Many teachers find that the staff room or a first-aid room works well, and you can ask your line manager to help you identify a private space. You don't have to tell everyone why you need it—you can just say you need a quiet place to take medication. It's also worth knowing that you have legal protections under the Equality Act, so your school has a duty to make reasonable adjustments to support you. Would it help if I noted down that you'd like to discuss this with your diabetes team when you're closer to returning to work?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Yes, please note that down. I'd feel better talking it through with them before I go back.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: I'll definitely note that down. Now, let's talk about your support network. You mentioned your sister lives nearby—does she know about your diagnosis, and is she someone you can call if you need help or just to talk?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Yes, Daniella knows. She's been really supportive, checking in on me. I can definitely call her if I need to.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's wonderful to hear. Having someone supportive nearby makes a big difference. It might be worth having a conversation with her about what to do if you have a severe hypo and can't treat yourself—like how to use the glucagon kit if you have one, or when to call 999. Do you have a glucagon kit at home, and does Daniella know how to use it?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: I don't have a glucagon kit. I'm not sure what that is, to be honest.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's okay—it's not something everyone knows about. Glucagon is an emergency injection that can be given to someone who is unconscious or unable to swallow due to a severe hypo. It's prescribed by your doctor, and it's a good idea to have one at home and to show a family member or close friend how to use it. I'll make a note to ask your diabetes team about getting you a glucagon kit and arranging for your sister to be shown how to use it. In the meantime, it's also important that Daniella knows to call 999 if you're unconscious or having a seizure and can't be woken. Does that sound like something you'd be comfortable talking to her about?

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Yes, I can talk to her about that. I'd feel better knowing she'd know what to do if something happened.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: That's a really good step. Now, let's talk about your logbook. I noticed you have one with you—can I take a look at the readings you've been recording? It will help me understand your patterns and see if there's anything we need to adjust.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Sure, here it is. I've been writing down my numbers, but I'm not sure if I'm doing it right.

actual_timeline.speaker: nurse
actual_timeline.text: Thank you. Let me have a look at what you've recorded so far.

actual_timeline.speaker: patient
actual_timeline.text: Okay.
